body.text: 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2) defines in-house research expenses for the federal research tax credit: wages for qualified services, supplies used in qualified research, and amounts paid for the right to use computers. U.S. taxpayers whose activities pass the § 41(d) four-part test may include these costs at 100%, unlike contract research, which is generally limited to 65%.

Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41(b)(2) (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)) establishes the statutory perimeter for quantifying internal corporate innovation expenditures eligible for the federal Credit for Increasing Research Activities. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A), in-house research expenses are strictly restricted to three exhaustive categories: (1) wages paid or incurred to an employee for qualified services performed by that employee (§ 41(b)(2)(A)(i)), (2) amounts paid or incurred for tangible supplies used in the conduct of qualified research (§ 41(b)(2)(A)(ii)), and (3) under Treasury regulations, amounts paid or incurred to another person for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research (§ 41(b)(2)(A)(iii)). Unlike contract research expenses under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)—which are statutorily limited to 65% of payments to third-party contractors (§ 41(b)(3)(A)), 75% of payments to qualified research consortia (§ 41(b)(3)(C)), or 100% of payments for qualified energy research to eligible small businesses, universities, or federal laboratories (§ 41(b)(3)(D))—in-house research expenses under § 41(b)(2) enter the qualified research expense (QRE) base at 100% of their eligible cost.

To qualify any expenditure as an in-house research expense under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2), a taxpayer must first demonstrate that the underlying technical activity satisfies the four-part statutory definition of "qualified research" in 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) and does not fall within the statutory exclusions of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4). Specifically, the activity must: (1) qualify for treatment as domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174A for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, pursuant to Public Law 119-21 (or as specified research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174 for prior periods) (§ 41(d)(1)(A)), meaning the expenditures represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the capability, method, or appropriate design of a product or improvement (26 C.F.R. § 1.174-2(a)(1)); (2) be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, fundamentally relying on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science (§ 41(d)(1)(B)(i); 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(4)); (3) be intended for application in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business (§ 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and § 41(d)(2)(B)); and (4) have "substantially all" (at least 80%) of its activities constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose relating to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality (§ 41(d)(1)(C), § 41(d)(3)(A), and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6)).

body.text: 1. Statutory Architecture of In-House Research Expenses Under 26 U.S.C. Section 41(b)

Internal Revenue Code Section 41(b)(1) defines "qualified research expenses" (QREs) as the sum of two categories of expenditures paid or incurred by a taxpayer during the taxable year in carrying on any trade or business of the taxpayer: (A) in-house research expenses and (B) contract research expenses. Under Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(a)(1), the phrase "in carrying on a trade or business" carries the exact same meaning for purposes of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(1) as it has for purposes of IRC § 162; consequently, expenses paid or incurred merely "in connection with" a trade or business within the meaning of IRC § 174(a) or § 174A(a) are not necessarily paid or incurred "in carrying on" a trade or business under § 41(b)(1). However, 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(4) provides a specific statutory exception exclusively for in-house research expenses of startup ventures: a taxpayer is treated as meeting the trade or business requirement of § 41(b)(1) with respect to in-house research expenses if, at the time such in-house research expenses are paid or incurred, the principal purpose of the taxpayer in making such expenditures is to use the results of the research in the active conduct of a future trade or business of the taxpayer or of one or more other persons who, together with the taxpayer, are treated as a single taxpayer under the controlled group aggregation rules of 26 U.S.C. § 41(f)(1).

The statutory distinction between in-house research expenses (§ 41(b)(2)) and contract research expenses (§ 41(b)(3)) directly governs the proportion of research outlays that enter the federal credit computation on IRS Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities). On the December 2023 revision of Form 6765 (which is also cross-referenced in Appendix B of the IRS LB&I ASC 730 Directive), QRE categories are entered on Lines 5–8 in Section A for the Regular Credit and Lines 24–27 in Section B for the Alternative Simplified Credit. On the redesigned December 2024 revision of Form 6765, taxpayers report itemized business-component wages (broken down into direct research on Line 50, direct supervision on Line 51, and direct support on Line 52, summed on Line 53), supplies (Line 54), computer rentals (Line 55), and contract research (Line 56) in Section G, aggregate those category totals in Section F on Lines 42–48 (with officers' wages included on Line 42 separately disclosed on Line 38 in Section E), and carry the total QRE figure from Line 48 to Line 5 (Section A, Regular Credit) or Line 20 (Section B, Alternative Simplified Credit). Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(A), contract research expenses paid or incurred to any person other than an employee of the taxpayer are generally limited to 65% of the qualified payment (increased to 75% for amounts paid to qualified tax-exempt scientific research consortia under § 41(b)(3)(C) and 100% for qualified energy research payments to eligible small businesses, universities, or federal laboratories under § 41(b)(3)(D)). By contrast, in-house research expenses under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2) are includable at 100% of the qualified expenditure, reflecting congressional policy to incentivize internal domestic scientific and engineering employment and direct laboratory experimentation.
Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A), the term "in-house research expenses" is defined exhaustively across three statutory clauses:

items: Employee Wages (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(i)): Any wages paid or incurred to an employee for qualified services performed by such employee.
Consumed Supplies (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii)): Any amount paid or incurred for supplies used in the conduct of qualified research.

Computer Rental / Right to Use Computers (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii)): Under regulations prescribed by the Secretary, any amount paid or incurred to another person for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research, subject to the statutory limitation in the flush language of § 41(b)(2)(A) that clause (iii) shall not apply to any amount to the extent that the taxpayer (or any person with whom the taxpayer must aggregate expenditures under § 41(f)(1)) receives or accrues any amount from any other person for the right to use substantially identical personal property.

body.text: Because 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A) is an exclusive statutory enumeration, the IRS Audit Techniques Guide (Credit for Increasing Research Activities (i.e. Research Tax Credit) IRC § 41 - Qualified Research Expenses, updated July 2, 2026) and Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(b)(1) and (c)(3) enforce a strict rule: if an expenditure is not explicitly set forth in § 41(b), a taxpayer may not claim it as a QRE. Consequently, general and administrative (G&A) expenses, facility overhead, equipment depreciation, amortization, travel, meals, entertainment, telephone expenses of researchers, relocation costs, facility or equipment rent/lease expenses (outside of qualifying computer time-sharing), professional dues, and patent or royalty license fees are categorically excluded from in-house research expenses, requiring a direct nexus between every claimed dollar and the physical conduct, first-line supervision, or direct support of qualified experimentation.

body.text: 2. Employee Wages for Qualified Services (26 U.S.C. Section 41(b)(2)(A)(i))
2.1 Statutory Definition of Wages and Section 3401(a) Nexus

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(D)(i), the term "wages" has the exact meaning given such term by 26 U.S.C. § 3401(a) for federal income tax withholding purposes. Consequently, eligible wages encompass all taxable remuneration for services performed by an employee for the employer as reported in Box 1 of IRS Form W-2, including base salaries, overtime, cash bonuses, and taxable stock option spreads upon exercise or disqualifying disposition. Conversely, the § 3401(a) definition excludes non-taxable fringe benefits (such as working condition fringes under IRC § 132(d) and § 3401(a)(19)), pre-tax 401(k) or cafeteria plan contributions, employer-paid health insurance premiums, and employer-portion payroll taxes (FICA and FUTA), even when paid to or on behalf of dedicated laboratory scientists performing 100% qualified research.

Two additional statutory rules in 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(D) modify the eligible wage base. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(D)(ii), in the case of a self-employed individual or owner-employee within the meaning of 26 U.S.C. § 401(c)(1) (encompassing sole proprietors and partners who perform personal services in a trade or business), the term "wages" includes the individual's net "earned income" as defined in 26 U.S.C. § 401(c)(2). Conversely, to prevent double-dipping across federal employment tax incentives, 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(D)(iii) explicitly mandates that the term "wages" shall not include any amount taken into account in determining the Work Opportunity Tax Credit (WOTC) under 26 U.S.C. § 51(a).
2.2 The Three Tiers of Qualified Services (26 U.S.C. Section 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-2(c))

Under Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(1), wages paid to or incurred for an employee constitute in-house research expenses only to the extent the wages were paid or incurred for "qualified services" performed by the employee. Both 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(1)–(3) divide qualified services into three distinct functional tiers (which are separately reported by business component on Lines 50, 51, and 52 of redesigned Form 6765, Section G):

items: Engaging in Qualified Research (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B)(i); 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(1)): Defined by regulation as "the actual conduct of qualified research (as in the case of a scientist conducting laboratory experiments)". In applied engineering and software contexts, this tier encompasses hands-on technical experimentation, such as writing experimental source code or formulating chemical compounds.

Direct Supervision (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B)(ii); 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(2)): Defined strictly as "the immediate supervision (first-line management) of qualified research (as in the case of a research scientist who directly supervises laboratory experiments, but who may not actually perform experiments)". Both the Treasury Regulation and the IRS Audit Techniques Guide enforce the "one-up" organizational boundary: "Direct supervision" does not include supervision by a higher-level manager to whom first-line managers report, even if that higher-level manager is a qualified research scientist. Higher-level executives qualify only to the extent they personally engage in direct technical ideation, hands-on experimentation, or immediate first-line supervision of researchers who have no intervening supervisor.

Direct Support (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B)(ii); 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(3)): Defined as services in the direct support of either (i) persons engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research, or (ii) persons who are directly supervising persons engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research. Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(3) enumerates four specific examples of qualifying direct support: a secretary typing reports describing laboratory results derived from qualified research; a laboratory worker cleaning equipment used in qualified research; a clerk compiling research data; and a machinist machining a part of an experimental model used in qualified research. Conversely, the regulation explicitly excludes general administrative services or other services only indirectly of benefit to research activities—such as payroll personnel preparing salary checks of laboratory scientists, an accountant accounting for research expenses, a janitor performing general cleaning of a research laboratory, or corporate officers engaged in supervising financial or personnel matters—and specifies that this exclusion applies regardless of whether those general administrative personnel are part of the research department or in a separate department. Furthermore, 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(3) clarifies that direct support does not include supervision; supervisory services constitute qualified services only to the extent provided in § 1.41-2(c)(2).

body.text: As emphasized in the IRS Audit Techniques Guide, audit determinations of whether an employee performed qualified services cannot rely on job titles, departmental cost-center labels, or academic degrees; credit eligibility depends solely on what the employee actually did during the specific taxable period.
2.3 The 80% Substantially All Wage Rule and Hypothetical Apportionment

When an employee performs both qualified services and nonqualified services during a taxable year, 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(1) dictates that only the amount of wages allocated to the performance of qualified services constitutes an in-house research expense. In the absence of another allocation method that the taxpayer can demonstrate to be more appropriate, the includable in-house wage expense is determined by multiplying the employee's total IRC § 3401(a) wages paid or incurred during the taxable year by the ratio of the total time actually spent by the employee in the performance of qualified services for the taxpayer to the total time spent by the employee in the performance of all services for the taxpayer during the taxable year.

However, the flush language of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) and Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2) establish a favorable statutory safe harbor known as the "substantially all" rule for employee wages. If "substantially all" of the services performed by an employee for the taxpayer during the taxable year consist of qualified services meeting the requirements of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B)(i) or (ii), then the term "qualified services" means all (100%) of the services performed by that employee for the taxpayer during the taxable year. Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2), services meeting § 41(b)(2)(B)(i) or (ii) constitute "substantially all" of the employee's services only if the wages allocated to those qualified services (on the time-ratio basis used for purposes of § 1.41-2(d)(1)) constitute at least 80% of the total wages paid to or incurred by the taxpayer for the employee during the taxable year.

Hypothetical Calculation — Application of the 80% Substantially All Wage Rule: Assume an engineering firm employs two full-time mechanical engineers during the taxable year, each working 2,000 total hours and earning $150,000.00 in Form W-2 Box 1 wages (IRC § 3401(a)).

For Engineer A (Meets the ≥80% Threshold), assume the engineer spends 1,640 hours designing and testing an experimental aerodynamic chassis (qualified services) and 360 hours on general administrative meetings and routine client support:

Because 82.0% is at least 80%, 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2) treats 100% of Engineer A's services as qualified services. The taxpayer includes the entire $150,000.00 of Engineer A's W-2 wages as in-house QREs, capturing the remaining 18.0% ($27,000.00) of routine or administrative time without reduction.
For Engineer B (Below the 80% Threshold), assume the engineer spends 1,500 hours on qualified experimental testing and 500 hours on post-production quality control and administrative duties:

Because 75.0% falls below the 80% threshold of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2), Engineer B's wages must be apportioned pro rata under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(1), yielding $150,000.00 × 0.75 = $112,500.00 in includable wage QREs (while excluding the remaining $37,500.00 attributable to nonqualified duties).
2.4 Judicial Precedents Governing Wage QRE Eligibility and Substantiation
Stock Option Spreads and Grant-Year Nexus: Apple Computer and Sun Microsystems

Federal tax litigation has established clear rules governing how equity-based employee compensation interacts with 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(i) and (D)(i). In Apple Computer, Inc. v. Commissioner, 98 T.C. 232 (1992), acq., 1992-2 C.B. 1, the IRS challenged Apple Computer's inclusion of the "spread" (the excess of the fair market value of the stock on the exercise date over the option exercise price) realized upon employees' exercise of nonqualified stock options (NSOs) as wage QREs under IRC § 44F (the statutory predecessor to IRC § 41). The Commissioner argued both that legislative history indicated option spreads were not intended to be treated as research wages and that the qualified services generating the options were performed in prior tax years (when the options were granted) rather than the tax year in which the options were exercised and the research credit was claimed. The Tax Court rejected both arguments, holding that because NSO spreads constitute compensation for services treated as wages subject to federal income tax withholding under IRC § 3401(a), they satisfy the statutory definition of wages under the research credit statute, and the fact that the underlying qualified services occurred in prior grant years does not disqualify the wage expense when incurred upon exercise (98 T.C. at 237–241).

In Sun Microsystems, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1995-69 (Docket No. 8976-91), acq., 1997-2 C.B. 1 (IRS Action on Decision CC-1997-010, Nov. 4, 1997), the Tax Court extended Apple Computer to Incentive Stock Options (ISOs). Between April 1983 and July 1986, Sun Microsystems granted ISOs meeting former IRC § 422A to employees engaged in qualified research services; in tax year 1987, employees sold shares acquired via ISO exercises prior to the expiration of the required statutory holding period, generating ordinary "spread income" under IRC § 421(b). The IRS issued a notice of deficiency removing the ISO disqualifying-disposition spread income from Sun Microsystems' 1987 QREs, relying on Rev. Rul. 71-52, 1971-1 C.B. 278, to argue that ISO disqualifying dispositions were not "wages" for withholding purposes. Finding neither support in Rev. Rul. 71-52 nor any basis for distinguishing Apple Computer, the Tax Court held that spread income attributable to disqualifying dispositions of ISO stock constitutes IRC § 3401(a) wages and is includable as a wage QRE under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(D). Following its acquiescence in Apple Computer and Sun Microsystems, the IRS instructs examiners in the Audit Techniques Guide to look to the grant year to determine whether the work performed by the employee constituted qualified services under § 41(b)(2)(B), and if so, to include the option spread in QRE wages in the year the option is exercised (for example, if an option is granted in 1997 for qualified research services and exercised in 2003, the examiner verifies that the 1997 services qualified and includes the spread in 2003 QRE wages).

Conversely, in IRS Chief Counsel Advice (Legal Advice Issued by Field Attorneys, LAFA) 20131102F (March 15, 2013), the IRS applied Apple Computer and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(1) to disallow Voluntary Separation Program (VSP) severance payments claimed as QREs. Although an earlier non-precedential Field Service Advice, FSA 199931012 (May 4, 1999), had concluded that workforce-reduction separation payments constituted IRC § 3401(a) wages eligible for § 41 treatment, FSA 199931012 had operated under the explicit, unverified assumption that every participating employee had performed only qualified research services during the entire duration of their employment with the taxpayer. In LAFA 20131102F, where the taxpayer allocated VSP severance payouts based solely on the percentage of qualified services performed by terminated employees in their final year of employment, Chief Counsel held that VSP payments are not deductible research or experimental expenditures in the "experimental or laboratory sense" under IRC § 174 and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1), were unreasonable in amount under former IRC § 174(e), and lacked the required nexus to qualified services under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(1) because severance formulas were tied to cumulative years of overall service and termination rather than the performance of qualified research.
Retroactive SME Estimates (Cohan Rule) and Executive Compensation Reasonableness: Suder v. Commissioner

In Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201 (Docket Nos. 14435-09, 14460-09, 6183-10, and 6210-10), following a three-week trial in Dallas, Texas generating over 3,500 pages of testimony and 170,000 pages of exhibits, the U.S. Tax Court addressed two recurring disputes under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(i): the substantiation of employee wage allocations in the absence of contemporaneous time-tracking, and the reasonableness ceiling on executive compensation. Eric G. Suder, the founder, CEO, and 90% shareholder of Estech Systems, Inc. (ESI)—an S corporation employing roughly 125 personnel (including approximately 40 engineers) with gross revenues of roughly $38.5 million by 2004 that developed business telephone hardware and software (private branch exchanges, auto-attendants, and voice mail systems)—and Douglas J. Boyd (President, COO, and 10% shareholder) claimed flow-through research tax credits for tax years 2004 through 2007 (with Suder claiming $445,987 in 2004, $440,306 in 2005, $454,526 in 2006, and $442,557 in 2007, and Boyd claiming $46,748 in 2004, $46,624 in 2005, $48,870 in 2006, and $48,378 in 2007). ESI's study provider identified 76 projects, which the parties litigated through a representative sample of 12 projects; the Tax Court held that 11 of the 12 representative projects satisfied the IRC § 41(d) four-part test (disallowing only one project involving routine bug-fixing of an existing commercial product). Wages constituted 95% of ESI's total claimed QREs (with supplies comprising the remaining 5%), and Suder's own compensation—exceeding $8.6 million annually, allocated at 75% to qualified services—accounted for roughly two-thirds of the company's entire wage QRE pool.

The Tax Court issued a two-part ruling on the wage QREs. First, on substantiation, ESI did not maintain contemporaneous hourly timesheets. Instead, Harvey Wende, ESI's Senior Vice President of Product Operations (2004–2006) and Senior Vice President of Product Development (2007), retrospectively estimated the percentage of time each employee spent on qualified services (including 75% for Suder, 25% for Boyd, and up to 100% for specific engineers and product managers). Distinguishing cases where witness testimony was self-serving and uncorroborated (such as Shami v. Commissioner), the Tax Court accepted Wende's percentage allocations under the rule of Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930) (and McFerrin v. Commissioner, 570 F.3d 672 (5th Cir. 2009)), because Wende and supporting engineering witnesses (including CTO Buzz Hansen and DSP firmware engineer Steven Wootton) possessed direct, first-hand knowledge of the employees' daily technical duties and provided a credible, detailed evidentiary basis for the time estimates.

Second, on executive pay reasonableness, although Suder worked 20 to 30 hours per week as ESI's "chief idea guy" and "product visionary" driving conceptual product architecture and alpha testing (while Boyd managed day-to-day manufacturing, tech support, sales, finance, and human resources), Suder's annual compensation ranged from 4.1 to 6 times (averaging 5.5 times) ESI's ordinary business income during 2004–2007 and moved up and down in lockstep proportion with Boyd's compensation according to their 90% and 10% stock ownership shares. Applying former IRC § 174(e)—which Congress enacted in the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1989 (P.L. 101-239, § 7110(d)) following Driggs v. United States, 706 F. Supp. 20 (N.D. Tex. 1989), to require that research expenditures be reasonable under the circumstances—and the multifactor reasonable compensation test of Owensby & Kritikos, Inc. v. Commissioner, 819 F.2d 1315 (5th Cir. 1987), the Tax Court held that Suder's compensation was unreasonable in part. Specifically, the court rejected the reasonable compensation computations of petitioners' expert witness, Brent M. Longnecker (who had opined that reasonable compensation for Suder at the 90th percentile totaled $11,035,735 in 2004, $11,321,086 in 2005, $12,179,498 in 2006, and $12,814,798 in 2007 by embedding hypothetical patent royalties of $8,669,645 to $10,170,891 per year based on consultations with Dr. Esber). The Tax Court excluded the royalty component because ESI never paid Suder through royalties, royalties are passive income rather than compensation for personal services rendered by an employee, and Suder was not named as an inventor on any new utility patent applications filed during 2004–2007 (having filed only a patent reissuance application on June 3, 2005, alongside 13 historical patents). Relying on the IRS's expert economist, Dr. Khalid Hafiz, the court capped Suder's allowable wage QREs at an arm's-length reasonable compensation level (while declining to impose IRC § 6662(a) accuracy-related penalties because petitioners acted in good faith reliance on their longtime CPA, Ms. Rogers).

Practitioners must note an important statutory evolution regarding IRC § 174(e), new IRC § 174A, and 26 C.F.R. § 1.174-2(a)(9). While former IRC § 174(e) operated as an explicit statutory cap during the 2004–2007 tax years in Suder, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (TCJA, P.L. 115-97, § 13206(a)) eliminated the statutory text of § 174(e) when it mandated 5-year domestic (and 15-year foreign) capitalization and amortization of specified research or experimental expenditures for tax years beginning after December 31, 2021. Furthermore, when Congress enacted Section 70302 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA, P.L. 119-21, enacted July 4, 2025) to permanently restore immediate expensing for domestic research or experimental expenditures under new IRC § 174A (and amended 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) to cross-reference § 174A) for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, Congress did not re-insert the statutory reasonableness text of former § 174(e) into IRC § 174A. Nevertheless, Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. § 1.174-2(a)(9) (promulgated in T.D. 8562 and redesignated in T.D. 9680)—which explicitly provides that "Section 174 applies to a research or experimental expenditure only to the extent that the amount of the expenditure is reasonable under the circumstances" (defined as the amount that "would ordinarily be paid for like activities by like enterprises under like circumstances") and recharacterizes excessive payments as "disguised dividends, gifts, loans, or similar payments"—remains codified in the Code of Federal Regulations, alongside the general compensation reasonableness standard of IRC § 162(a)(1).
Production Wages and the Process-of-Experimentation Substantially All Fraction: Little Sandy Coal and Intermountain Electronics

Taxpayers and auditors must carefully distinguish the 80% "substantially all" safe harbor for employee wages (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2)) from the separate 80% "substantially all" requirement for the process-of-experimentation test (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6)). Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6), "substantially all" of the research activities with respect to a business component constitute elements of a process of experimentation only if 80% or more of a taxpayer's research activities for that business component—measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis (such as employee hours)—constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose:

In Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), aff'g T.C. Memo. 2021-15, a shipbuilding subsidiary (Corn Island Shipyard, Inc.) claimed research tax credits across 11 custom vessel projects, litigated through two representative first-in-class "pilot models" (a custom tank barge and a dry dock), including the wages of production employees physically fabricating the vessels and the materials incorporated into them. In its memorandum opinion (T.C. Memo. 2021-15), the Tax Court had ruled that physical production activities (fabricating a physical component), direct supervision, and direct support could not be included in the numerator of the 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6) 80% fraction. On appeal, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit (62 F.4th 287) explicitly disagreed with the Tax Court's categorical exclusion of direct supervision, direct support, and pilot-model production activities from the numerator, clarifying that production staff wages and direct support or supervision may constitute elements of a process of experimentation and be included in the numerator if those activities genuinely form part of an evaluative scientific or engineering test.

Nevertheless, the Seventh Circuit affirmed the complete disallowance of the credit because the shipbuilder defined its business component overly broadly as the entire vessel (failing to apply the shrinking-back rule of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2) to isolate novel subcomponents) and relied on arbitrary, unsupported trial estimates rather than contemporaneous documentary evidence isolating experimental activities from routine fabrication, holding that "shortcut estimates of experimentation-related activities will not suffice... [s]omething more, such as documentation of time spent on such activities, is necessary". Subsequently, in Intermountain Electronics, Inc. v. Commissioner, Docket No. 11019-19 (U.S. Tax Court Order dated March 14, 2024)—where a Utah-based custom electrical distribution and transformer manufacturer claimed wage and supply QREs for tax years 2012–2015 on custom equipment treated as pilot models under 26 C.F.R. § 1.174-2(a)(4)—the Tax Court denied the IRS's motion for partial summary judgment. Aligning with the Seventh Circuit's rationale, the Tax Court formally confirmed that Little Sandy Coal "does not foreclose production expenses from being included in the numerator of the substantially all equation" as a matter of law, leaving the qualification of pilot-model production wages and supplies to be established through detailed project documentation at trial.
3. Consumed Supplies in the Conduct of Qualified Research (26 U.S.C. Section 41(b)(2)(A)(ii))
3.1 Tangibility, Direct Consumption, and Excluded Indirect Costs

The second category of in-house research expenses under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) encompasses "any amount paid or incurred for supplies used in the conduct of qualified research". Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(C), the term "supplies" is statutorily defined as any tangible property other than: (i) land or improvements to land (§ 41(b)(2)(C)(i)), and (ii) property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation (§ 41(b)(2)(C)(ii)).

Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(b)(1) establishes the nexus requirement for supplies: supplies and personal property are used in the conduct of qualified research only if they are used in the performance of qualified services (as defined in 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B), but without regard to the last sentence thereof containing the 80% "substantially all" wage rule) by an employee of the taxpayer (or by a person acting in a capacity similar to that of an employee of the taxpayer). Consequently, even if an engineer satisfies the 80% wage safe harbor of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2) so that 100% of the engineer's W-2 wages qualify, tangible supplies consumed by that engineer during the 15% of time spent on non-qualified routine maintenance do not qualify as supply QREs. Furthermore, 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(b)(1) and the IRS Audit Techniques Guide mandate that expenditures for supplies or for the use of personal property that constitute indirect research expenditures or general and administrative (G&A) expenses—including G&A costs related to self-constructed supplies, shipping, travel, meals, entertainment, telephone bills of researchers, relocation costs, asset leasing fees, professional dues, and royalty or software license fees—do not qualify as in-house supply QREs.
3.2 The Extraordinary Utilities Exception (26 C.F.R. Section 1.41-2(b)(2)(ii))

Under the general rule of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(b)(2)(i), amounts paid or incurred for utilities such as water, electricity, and natural gas used in a building in which qualified research is performed are treated as expenditures for general and administrative expenses (for instance, electricity used for general laboratory lighting or facility heating, ventilation, and air conditioning). However, 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(b)(2)(ii) carves out a narrow regulatory exception for "extraordinary expenditures":

"To the extent the taxpayer can establish that the special character of the qualified research required additional extraordinary expenditures for utilities, the additional expenditures shall be treated as amounts paid or incurred for supplies used in the conduct of qualified research."

The regulation specifically cites amounts paid for electricity used in operating high-energy equipment for qualified research (such as laser or nuclear research) as an example of an extraordinary additional expenditure for electricity that can be segregated from baseline facility utility bills and claimed at 100% as an in-house supply QRE under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii).
3.3 The Depreciable Property Exclusion: TG Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner

Because 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(C)(ii) excludes "property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation" (mirroring the IRC § 174(c) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.174-2(b)(1) rule that expenditures for the acquisition or improvement of depreciable property used in connection with research are not deductible under § 174), the IRS frequently challenges tangible prototype, die, and tooling outlays as depreciable capital assets.

In TG Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner, 133 T.C. 278 (2009), the taxpayer manufactured injection-molded automotive components and incurred costs to design, develop, and purchase complex production molds from third-party toolmakers to produce parts for its automotive customers. For the molds at issue, TG Missouri sold ownership of the completed production molds to its customers (who held the economic ownership interest while TG Missouri retained physical possession on its factory floor solely to manufacture automotive parts for the customers) and claimed the mold costs as supply QREs under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) and (C). The IRS disallowed the costs, arguing that injection molds inherently possess a physical useful life exceeding one year and were depreciable property in the hands of the automotive customers, rendering them "of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation" under § 41(b)(2)(C)(ii) and IRC § 174(c).

The Tax Court ruled in favor of the taxpayer (133 T.C. at 288–297), holding that the statutory phrase "property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation" under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(C)(ii) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.174-2(b) refers strictly to whether the property is subject to an allowance for depreciation in the hands of the taxpayer claiming the credit, not in the hands of a third-party customer. Because TG Missouri sold the molds to its customers rather than holding the economic ownership interest as capital assets subject to depreciation in its own trade or business, the molds were not depreciable property in TG Missouri's hands and qualified in full as in-house supply QREs.
3.4 Process Versus Product Research Supplies: Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner

While TG Missouri confirmed that selling an experimental tool or prototype to a customer does not disqualify its material cost under § 41(b)(2)(C)(ii), Union Carbide Corp. & Subsidiaries v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50 (97 T.C.M. (CCH) 1207), aff'd, 697 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2012), established a strict boundary against claiming ordinary raw materials consumed during commercial-scale manufacturing process research. Union Carbide originally claimed research credits for its laboratory and pilot-plant research, but subsequently petitioned the Tax Court to claim additional research credits across 106 manufacturing plant projects (litigated via 5 sample projects), of which the Tax Court found two projects constituted qualified process research: (1) the Amoco anticoking project, where Union Carbide pretreated high-temperature (1,400°F to 1,650°F) hydrocarbon cracking coils twice with an experimental compound to inhibit coke buildup while thermally cracking raw feedstock into olefins; and (2) the UCAT-J project, where Union Carbide conducted 19 commercial production runs testing a new catalyst four times more active than its standard M-1 catalyst to manufacture polyethylene resin for customer orders. Union Carbide sold all resulting aim-grade and off-grade olefins and polyethylene resin in the ordinary course of business and sought to claim the massive raw material costs of the hydrocarbon feedstock and resin ingredients consumed during those full-scale production runs as supply QREs under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) (along with plant operator wages under § 41(b)(2)(A)(i)).

The Tax Court disallowed the raw material supply claims (and associated plant operator production wages), and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed (697 F.3d 104) on three independent grounds:

items: Indirect / Ordinary Production Cost Exclusion (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(b)(1)): Reading the word "used" in its full statutory context under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) alongside 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(b)(1), raw materials used to manufacture finished goods for commercial sale—which would have been purchased regardless of whether the taxpayer was evaluating an experimental manufacturing process—constitute indirect research expenditures or ordinary inventory/cost-of-goods-sold outlays (IRC § 162), not supplies used in the conduct of qualified research.

Special Statutory Rule for Plant Processes (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(C)): Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(C), a "plant process, machinery, or technique for commercial production of a business component shall be treated as a separate business component (and not as part of the business component being produced)". Accordingly, when the business component undergoing experimentation is the manufacturing plant process rather than the manufactured product itself, feedstocks that form the commercial product do not become experimental supplies merely because the production run is being monitored for process improvements.

Avoidance of Statutory Windfalls: The Second Circuit emphasized that IRC § 41 is designed to incentivize incremental research outlays that a taxpayer would not otherwise incur, and subsidizing ordinary raw material inventory that would have been purchased regardless of any research would confer an unintended windfall on the taxpayer.

body.text: 3.5 Pilot Models and the Commercial Production Cutoff

In response to post-TG Missouri and Union Carbide disputes over prototypes and custom-built items, the Treasury Department amended 26 C.F.R. § 1.174-2 in July 2014 (T.D. 9680) to codify explicit regulatory rules for pilot models and the shrinking-back of product components. Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.174-2(a)(4), a "pilot model" is defined as "any representation or model of a product that is produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty concerning the product during the development or improvement of the product," explicitly including "a fully-functional representation or model of the product or, to the extent paragraph (a)(5) of this section applies, a component of the product".

Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.174-2(a)(1), qualification depends on the nature of the activity to which the expenditures relate rather than the nature of the product or the level of technological advancement it represents; the ultimate success, failure, sale, or use of the product or pilot model is irrelevant to its eligibility under IRC § 174 (and § 174A), and costs may qualify even if paid or incurred after physical production begins so long as they are paid or incurred before uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of the product is eliminated. However, two strict cutoffs terminate supply QRE eligibility. First, under 26 C.F.R. § 1.174-2(a)(2), except where the shrinking-back or component rule of 26 C.F.R. § 1.174-2(a)(5) applies to isolate a specific uncertain subcomponent, costs paid or incurred in the production of a product after the elimination of uncertainty concerning its development or improvement are ineligible commercial production costs (as illustrated in the regulatory examples, where $10,000 of materials and labor to build a pilot model of a custom machine plus $1,000 of testing to resolve design uncertainty qualify under § 174, whereas $20,000 subsequently spent to fabricate the machine for sale to the customer after design uncertainty is resolved does not qualify). Second, under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(A), any research conducted after the beginning of commercial production of the business component—once the component meets basic functional and economic design specifications and passes validation testing—is statutorily excluded from "qualified research".
4. Computer Rental Fees and Cloud Computing Environments (26 U.S.C. Section 41(b)(2)(A)(iii))

The third exhaustive category of in-house research expenses under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) consists of, "under regulations prescribed by the Secretary, any amount paid or incurred to another person for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research". Originally enacted when companies leased time-sharing processing capacity on off-site mainframe supercomputers, this provision now serves as the statutory basis for claiming third-party cloud computing infrastructure costs—such as Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform (GCP)—incurred for software compilation, load-testing simulations, sandbox virtual machines, and artificial intelligence or machine learning model training.

Under Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(b)(4), for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1985, amounts paid or incurred for the use or lease of personal property are not qualified research expenses, except for amounts paid or incurred to another person for the right to use (time-sharing) computers in the conduct of qualified research that satisfy a strict three-part conjunctive test:

items: Third-Party Ownership and Operation: The computer must be owned and operated by someone other than the taxpayer;
Off-Premises Location: The computer must be located off the taxpayer's physical premises; and
Non-Primary User Requirement: The taxpayer must not be the primary user of the computer.

body.text: In addition, the flush language of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A) imposes an anti-conduit limitation: clause (iii) does not apply to any amount to the extent that the taxpayer (or any controlled group member aggregated under § 41(f)(1)) receives or accrues any amount from any other person for the right to use substantially identical personal property. In practice, technology taxpayers must maintain granular cloud billing segregation—isolating off-premises, shared-tenancy cloud server instances dedicated to pre-production development, staging, and experimental testing (§ 41(b)(2)(A)(iii)), while strictly excluding on-premises leased hardware, dedicated single-tenant bare-metal servers where the taxpayer is the primary user (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(b)(4)), software-as-a-service (SaaS) office productivity licenses (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(b)(1)), and live customer-facing commercial production hosting environments (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(A)).
5. IRS Administrative Safe Harbor: The LB&I ASC 730 Directive

Because auditing the 26 U.S.C. § 41(d) four-part test and § 41(b)(2) cost allocations on a project-by-project basis consumes substantial examination resources, the IRS Large Business and International (LB&I) Division introduced an administrative safe harbor on September 11, 2017 (Guidance for Allowance of the Credit for Increasing Research Activities under I.R.C. § 41 for Taxpayers that Expense Research and Development Costs on their Financial Statements pursuant to ASC 730, Control No. LB&I-04-0917-005), and subsequently refined it on September 10, 2020, via the Revised ASC 730 Directive (Control No. LB&I-04-0820-0016, effective for original timely filed returns for tax periods ending on or after July 31, 2020, and codified in Internal Revenue Manual IRM 4.30.2.11.3 and 4.30.2.11.4).
5.1 Eligibility Criteria and Scope

Under LB&I-04-0820-0016, LB&I examiners will not challenge a taxpayer's "Adjusted ASC 730 Financial Statement R&D" QREs (reported in Column A of Appendix B) if the taxpayer satisfies four cumulative eligibility requirements. First, the taxpayer must be an LB&I taxpayer with total assets equal to or greater than $10,000,000. Second, the taxpayer must prepare Certified Audited Financial Statements (CAFS) in accordance with U.S. Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) and use those exact same CAFS to reconcile book income to federal taxable income on Schedule M-3 (checking the Part I, Line 4(b) GAAP accounting standard box, and reconciling to Form 1120 Schedule M-3, Part III, Line 35, or Form 1120-S / Form 1065 Schedule M-3, Part III, Line 29). Third, the CAFS must display currently expensed Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) ASC 730 (Research and Development) costs either as a standalone line item on the income statement or separately stated in a footnote to the CAFS. Fourth, the taxpayer must attach completed Appendices A, B, C, and D (with Appendix A signed under penalties of perjury pursuant to IRC § 6062) to its original timely filed tax return (including extensions) and retain underlying general ledger (GL) account details, cost-center lists, organization charts, and Form W-2 payroll records for production upon an Information Document Request (IDR).
5.2 Mechanical Reconciliation Steps (Appendices C and D)

While FASB ASC 730 and IRC § 41 both address research and development, book ASC 730 R&D is broader geographically and functionally than 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2). The Directive requires a structured mechanical subtraction and wage-substitution workflow across Appendix C and Appendix D to convert book R&D into statutory in-house QREs:

cells: Step 1: U.S. Financial Statement Baseline (App. C, Lines 1–2)

Start with total CAFS R&D expense (Line 1); subtract foreign entity R&D accounts (e.g., Controlled Foreign Corporations, Line 1a) and non-consolidated U.S. entities filing separate federal returns (Line 1b) to yield U.S. Financial Statement R&D (Line 2), reconciled to Schedule M-3.
Establishes the audited U.S. GAAP book baseline for the consolidated federal tax return group and removes foreign subsidiary accounts barred by IRC § 41(d)(4)(F).
Step 2: Non-ASC 730 Subtractions (2020 Revised App. C, Lines 3a–4)

Subtract non-ASC 730 book R&D expenses included in Financial Statement R&D (such as software development costs accounted for under ASC 985-20 or cloud computing/internal-use software standards on Line 3a, and routine/ongoing commercial production engineering on Line 3b) to yield U.S. ASC 730 Financial Statement R&D (Line 4).
Restricts the administrative safe harbor strictly to costs expensed under FASB ASC 730 definitions and removes post-production engineering barred by IRC § 41(d)(4)(A).
Step 3: Non-IRC § 174 & Non-IRC § 41 Exclusions (App. C, Lines 5–11a)

Subtract § 174 excluded GL accounts (Line 5: quality control testing, efficiency surveys, management studies, consumer surveys, advertising/promotions, patent/model acquisitions, literary/historical research, excessive amounts, and land/depreciable property); subtract non-wage/non-supply/non-contract GL accounts (Line 6: depreciation, amortization, shipping, travel, training, rent, overhead, G&A); subtract research performed to comply with customer contracts/agreements regardless of whether funded (Line 7), non-employee contract research costs (Line 8), foreign in-house research by U.S. employees (Line 9), and prototype overhead, patent costs, and severance pay (Line 10).

Filters out activities barred by IRC § 174 / § 174A and § 41(d)(4) (including foreign research under § 41(d)(4)(F) and contract/funded research under § 41(d)(4)(H)), and removes overhead, depreciation, rent, and severance excluded from in-house QREs under § 41(b)(2), 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(b)(1), and LAFA 20131102F.
Step 4: W-2 Wage Substitution & 95% Safe Harbor Tiers (App. C, Lines 12–16 & App. D, Lines 1–6)

Subtract remaining book GAAP wages, wage-related accounts, and book stock-based compensation (Lines 12–14); add back IRC § 3401(a) Form W-2 wages and W-2 stock option spreads for employees charged to U.S. ASC 730 cost centers at 95% for Qualified Individual Contributors (QICs) (employees who do not manage any other taxpayer employees, Line 15 / App. D Lines 1–3) and 95% for 1st Level Supervisor Managers (managers who directly manage only QICs, Line 16 / App. D Lines 4–6).

Harmonizes book payroll accruals and GAAP ASC 718 stock expense with 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(D)(i) (§ 3401(a) W-2 wages) and applies a standardized 5% administrative haircut for incidental non-qualified administrative tasks.
Step 4 (Cont.): Upper Level Managers' (ULM) 10% Limit & Step 5 Total (App. C, Lines 17–22 & App. D, Line 7)

Cap Upper Level Managers (ULMs) (managers above 1st Level Supervisors) at the lesser of: (a) 10% of the combined 95%-adjusted W-2 wages and stock options of QICs and 1st Level Supervisors, or (b) 100% of actual ULM W-2 wages/stock options charged to U.S. ASC 730 cost centers (Line 17 / App. D Line 7). Sum adjusted supplies/computers (Line 11a) and net wage adjustments (Line 18) on Line 19, and break out into Wages (Line 20), Supplies (Line 21), and Computer Rental (Line 22).

Imposes a mechanical ceiling on executive/higher-tier management claims (addressing audit controversies like Suder v. Commissioner). Cliff Rule: If a taxpayer elects to claim more than the 10% ULM Limit, ULM wages in the Directive drop to $0 on App. C Line 17 and must be substantiated outside the safe harbor in App. B, Columns B & C.

Computing the allowable Directive wage QREs step by step under Appendix D:

items: QIC Safe Harbor Wages (App. D, Lines 1–3): $4,000,000.00 × 95% = $3,800,000.00
1st Level Supervisor Safe Harbor Wages (App. D, Lines 4–6): $1,000,000.00 × 95% = $950,000.00
Combined QIC and 1st Level Supervisor Subtotal: $3,800,000.00 + $950,000.00 = $4,750,000.00
ULM 10% Limit (App. D, Line 7): Lesser of $800,000.00 actual ULM wages or 10% of $4,750,000.00 ($475,000.00) = $475,000.00

body.text: 6. State R&D Tax Credit Conformity and Divergence Frameworks

While state research tax credit statutes overwhelmingly incorporate the federal in-house expense categories of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2) (wages, supplies, and computer rental) and the § 41(d) four-part test, states impose strict geographic nexus walls, bespoke credit rate structures, and distinct IRC conformity dates.
6.1 California Revenue and Taxation Code (R&TC) Section 23609
Geographic Nexus and Sales Tax Exemption Exclusion

California administers its corporate Research and Development Credit under California Revenue and Taxation Code (R&TC) § 23609 (and under R&TC § 17052.12 for personal income tax filers and pass-through shareholders via Franchise Tax Board [FTB] Form 3523). Under R&TC § 23609(c)(2), California enforces an absolute geographic boundary: the terms "qualified research" and "basic research" include only research conducted in California. Consequently, when a multi-state engineering team collaborates on a single software module across California and Texas, only the wages of employees physically performing qualified services within California, tangible supplies physically consumed in California, and qualifying computer rentals attributable to research conducted in California enter the California QRE calculation. Additionally, R&TC § 23609(c)(1) modifies IRC § 41(b)(1) to exclude from California QREs any amount paid or incurred on or after January 1, 1999, for tangible personal property that is eligible for the exemption from sales or use tax under R&TC § 6378 (property used primarily in teleproduction or other postproduction services, or to maintain, repair, measure, or test such property).
California Office of Tax Appeals (OTA) Substantiation Precedents

The California Franchise Tax Board (FTB) and the California Office of Tax Appeals (OTA) subject in-house wage and supply QRE claims to rigorous evidentiary scrutiny. In Appeal of Electronic Data Systems Corporation & Subsidiaries, 2023-OTA-540 (OTA Case Nos. 19014166, 19125644, and 22039829, heard June 14, 2023, Nonprecedential), the appellant claimed $35,277,616 in total California tax refunds across tax years 2003 through 2008 ($20,800 for 2003; $3,151,075 for 2004; $5,174,624 for 2005; $5,596,361 for 2006; $8,012,409 for 2007; $10,000,523 for the short tax year ending August 26, 2008; and $3,321,824 for the short tax year ending August 28/29, 2008, following its acquisition by Hewlett-Packard Company). These refund claims were based on $246,728,594 in originally claimed California QREs for tax years 2005 through the two 2008 short tax years ($53,685,304 in 2005; $73,786,769 in 2006; $71,805,103 in 2007; $46,863,177 for TYE August 26, 2008; and $588,241 for TYE August 28, 2008), which the appellant subsequently reduced by 45% across the board to match its federal IRS audit concession.

For the 2003 and 2004 tax years (where FTB had previously allowed $615,722 and $666,376 in research credits on audit), the OTA held that it lacked jurisdiction over the regular research credit because the appellant's 2012 refund claims had only claimed the Alternative Incremental Credit (AIC/AIRC), and held that the appellant was barred from claiming the AIC because it had not elected the AIC on its original timely filed 2003 and 2004 returns. For the 2005–2008 tax years (where jurisdiction over the regular credit was established via 2020 supplemental refund claims totaling $32,105,741), the FTB conceded $75,966,096 in reduced California qualified wages for the 2006–2008 tax years at the hearing, but contested the 2005 wages and all 2005–2008 supply and contractor QREs. The appellant had tracked project costs using Financial Identification (FID) codes and attempted to substantiate its remaining QREs using unsigned, undated year-end consultant surveys, allocating supplies ($142,014 in a sample FID) by "man-months," estimating contractor allocations ($125,000 in the sample FID) via a financial employee's experience, and apportioning costs to California using a statewide W-2/GL payroll ratio. The OTA ruled in favor of the FTB, rejecting the unverified ratio estimations and holding that the retrospective surveys lacked contemporaneous documentary support, failed to verify the underlying supply and contractor costs, and failed to demonstrate that at least 80% of the California research activities for each business component constituted a process of experimentation conducted in California.

Similarly, in Appeals of Charles Walden and Deborah Anderson, Charles Walden, and Walden Structures, Inc., 2018-OTA-209 (OTA Case Nos. 18010221, 18010222, and 18010223, issued November 28, 2018, Nonprecedential), evaluating six agreed-upon sample custom modular building projects for tax years 2003 through 2006 (Bramasole, Welk Resort, Mammoth Lakes Foundation Dorms, Mosque 1 & 2, Genentech, and Ynez Elementary), the OTA required project-by-project proof of the IRC § 41(d)(1) four-part test. The OTA held that the taxpayers failed to prove qualified research for five of the six sample projects (several of which relied on the taxpayer's existing standard S-1000 structural engineering package), while sustaining qualification for one project—the Mosque 1 & 2 military training structures, where heavy rooftop domes, large floor and ceiling cutouts, highway transportability constraints, and breachable doors created genuine structural design uncertainty not resolved by available engineering data, and which was not barred by the IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) adaptation or § 41(d)(4)(C) duplication exclusions.
Correction on California IRC Conformity Date, Credit Rates, and Repeal of the AIRC (2025 Update)

First, for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025, California updated its general IRC conformity date from January 1, 2015, to January 1, 2025 (as reflected in the 2025 Instructions for Form FTB 3523). Second, California continues to provide a 15% Regular Research Credit on California QREs exceeding the California base period amount (R&TC § 23609(b)(2)), plus a 24% Basic Research Credit for C corporations making cash payments under written contracts to qualified universities or scientific research organizations in California. Under R&TC § 23803(a) and IRC § 41(e)(7)(E), S corporations are ineligible for the 24% basic research credit, may utilize only one-third (1/3) of the regular or alternative simplified research credit against the 1.5% entity-level franchise tax (3.5% for financial S corporations) while disregarding the remaining two-thirds (2/3) with no entity-level carryover, and pass through 100% of the credit calculated under the Personal Income Tax Law (R&TC § 17052.12) to their shareholders on Schedule K-1 (100S).

Third, pursuant to the 2025 amendments to R&TC §§ 17052.12 and 23609, the former three-tier Alternative Incremental Credit (R&TC § 23609(h)(1), which provided rates of 1.49%, 1.98%, and 2.48% for pre-2025 tax years) is repealed and no longer available for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025. In its place, California now conforms with modifications to the federal Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) under IRC § 41(c)(4), allowing taxpayers to elect a California ASC equal to 3% of current-year California QREs that exceed 50% of the average California QREs for the three preceding taxable years (or 1.3% of current-year California QREs if the taxpayer had no California QREs in any one of the three preceding taxable years). Taxpayers who previously elected the repealed AIRC do not automatically default to either method and must affirmatively elect either the 15% regular credit or the new 3% / 1.3% ASC on Form FTB 3523.

Fourth, even under the January 1, 2025 IRC conformity update, California explicitly does not conform to the federal TCJA (P.L. 115-97, § 13206(a)) 5-year capitalization and amortization rules for IRC § 174 research and experimental expenses. California continues to permit immediate 100% deductibility of R&D expenses (reduced by the amount of the current-year California research credit claimed under R&TC § 24440 unless the taxpayer elects the reduced credit under IRC § 280C(c)). Unused California research credits carry forward indefinitely until exhausted (R&TC § 23609(f)), subject for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2024, and before January 1, 2027, to California's $5,000,000 annual business credit utilization limitation (with an irrevocable election available on Form FTB 3870 to claim disallowed credits as a 20%-per-year refundable credit over a 5-year period beginning three years after the election).
6.2 New York: Life Sciences R&D Credit, Excelsior Jobs Program, R&D ITC, and QETC Guidance

New York State administers multiple innovation tax incentives through Empire State Development (ESD) and the New York State Department of Taxation and Finance (DTF), all of which enforce a strict geographic nexus requiring eligible expenditures to be physically incurred within New York State. Under the Life Sciences Research and Development Tax Credit Program (N.Y. Tax Law §§ 43, 210-B(52), and 606(hhh); Forms CT-648 and IT-648), available to certified "new businesses" (under N.Y. Tax Law § 210-B(1)(f) or § 606(a)(10), requiring among other criteria that the applicant not have been a taxpayer in New York for more than 5 tax years and not have been a related person under IRC § 465(b)(3)(C) within the preceding 60 months to an existing life sciences or R&D entity) for up to 3 consecutive years (for taxable years beginning before January 1, 2028), New York provides a fully refundable credit equal to 15% of qualified NYS R&D expenditures for companies employing 10 or more full-time persons during the tax year (working at least 35 hours per week, averaged across March 31, June 30, September 30, and December 31, excluding general executive officers under N.Y. Tax Law § 43(g)), or 20% for companies employing fewer than 10 full-time persons. The credit is capped at $500,000 per year per company or combined group ($1.5 million lifetime cap; $10 million statewide annual allocation limit awarded in order of application filing date) and cannot reduce corporate tax below the fixed dollar minimum tax or offset the MTA surcharge, with any excess refunded in cash (without interest) or applied to the following year's tax. Crucially for 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2) analysis, N.Y. Tax Law § 43(c)(4) and ESD program guidelines explicitly state that while R&D expenditures are defined by reference to federal QREs under IRC § 41(b) incurred in New York on or after January 1, 2018, contract research expenses under IRC § 41(b)(1)(B) and § 41(b)(3) are explicitly excluded—meaning the New York Life Sciences R&D Tax Credit is restricted 100% to in-house research expenses under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2) (wages, supplies, and computer rental) incurred in New York.

Under the Excelsior Jobs Program Research and Development Tax Credit (N.Y. Tax Law §§ 31 and 210-B(31)), certified strategic-industry firms participating in the Excelsior Jobs Program over a benefit schedule of up to 10 years (or up to 20 years across two 10-year phases for Green CHIPS projects creating at least 500 net new jobs and $3 billion in qualified investment in Phase Two) may claim a fully refundable credit equal to 50% of the portion of the taxpayer's federal IRC § 41 credit attributable to research activities conducted in New York State, capped at 6% of NYS research expenditures for standard projects, 7% for semiconductor supply chain projects, and 8% for green or Green CHIPS projects. Additionally, for corporate franchise taxpayers under Article 9-A, New York offers an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) for R&D Property (Form CT-46) on tangible depreciable property placed in service in New York and used for R&D in the experimental or laboratory sense at an optional rate of 9% for C corporations (or 7% for New York S corporations passed through to shareholders). While non-refundable for established corporations (qualified "new businesses" under N.Y. Tax Law § 210-B.1(f) may elect a cash refund without interest), unused R&D ITC carries forward for up to 15 tax years for C corporations and 10 tax years for S corporation shareholders under Article 22.

Furthermore, in technical memoranda TSB-M-99(2.1)C and TSB-M-00(2)I governing Qualified Emerging Technology Company (QETC) credits under N.Y. Tax Law §§ 210-B(7) and 606(q) and N.Y. Public Authorities Law (PAL) § 3102-e (for companies located in New York State with total annual product sales of $10 million or less), the DTF links the state's R&D funds ratio (requiring a ratio of R&D funds to net sales of at least 3.0%, representing the lesser of the National Science Foundation [NSF] average ratios for federally funded [3.5%] and non-federally funded [3.0%] R&D companies) and eligible R&D activities directly to the NSF Survey of Industry Research and Development (now the Business R&D Survey [BRDS], referenced on Form DTF-621-I). Both memoranda reinforce the exclusion of routine product testing, quality control, pre-production toolmaking and tool tryout, detailed construction drawings and blueprints, market research, efficiency surveys, sales promotion, and social sciences or psychology research.
6.3 State-Level Jurisprudence and Statutory Rules in Indiana, Idaho, and Rhode Island
Indiana: Correcting the Conflation of Tell City Boatworks and System Technologies

In Tell City Boatworks, Inc. v. Indiana Department of State Revenue, 162 N.E.3d 603 (Ind. Tax Ct. 2020) (Cause No. 18T-TA-00004, decided December 18, 2020)—the first research credit trial before the Indiana Tax Court under Ind. Code § 6-3.1-4-1 (which incorporates IRC § 41)—a custom river barge and vessel builder located along the Ohio River in Tell City, Indiana, claimed Indiana research expense credits for the fiscal tax year ended June 30, 2011 ("2010 tax year") across custom vessel projects, four of which were examined in the opinion: Project 112 (a 230' × 62' × 14' industrial cutter dredge built for Weeks Marine, Inc.), Project 107 (a 150' × 69' × 10' crane barge for Brennan Marine), Project 109 (a 200' × 69' × 10' crane barge), and Project 111 (a 100' × 50' × 7.5' deck barge for Mulzer modified from Hull No. 155). Tell City operated as an overflow yard 11 river miles from its sister company, Corn Island Shipyard, Inc. (both owned by the Foertsch family, but maintained as separate legal entities with separate employees, bank accounts, and accounting systems). The Indiana Tax Court denied the credit in full: on Project 112, Tell City failed the Business Component Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and § 41(d)(2)(B)) because Weeks Marine contracted directly with Corn Island—not Tell City—and Corn Island assumed full launch-damage liability and held the vessel for sale, while Tell City acted merely as an assembly subcontractor with no substantiated contract assignment; and on Projects 107, 109, and 111, although Tell City passed the Technological Information Test (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(4)), it failed the Process of Experimentation Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6)) by failing to prove with cost or time breakdowns that at least 80% of its activities constituted a systematic trial-and-error process of experimentation.

Conversely, it was the U.S. Tax Court in System Technologies, Inc. v. Commissioner, Docket No. 12211-21 (Order dated January 3, 2025), that addressed the interplay between Indiana state contract law and the funded research exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) (and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d)). The taxpayer engineered and manufactured custom industrial finishing and automotive coating systems (such as robotic paint applications, pre-treatment solutions, and ultraviolet curing systems) across six projects under customer purchase orders governed by Indiana law for tax years 2015 through 2018. The IRS moved for partial summary judgment, arguing that the contracts lacked express success-contingent payment terms and that their limited warranty clauses foreclosed buyer refund remedies. In its January 3, 2025 Order, the U.S. Tax Court denied the IRS's partial summary judgment motion, holding that under Indiana contract law, the warranty provisions did not override the buyer's statutory and common-law remedies to demand a refund in the event of non-delivery or total breach—meaning payment remained contingent on research success and was not "funded research" on the summary judgment record.
Idaho: Administrative Application of Suder, Little Sandy Coal, and Union Carbide

Under Idaho Code § 63-3029G, Idaho allows a non-refundable credit for increasing research activities physically conducted in Idaho by expressly adopting the QRE and four-part test definitions of IRC § 41. In Idaho State Tax Commission Docket No. 2-117-100-544 (decision upholding a December 1, 2023 Notice of Deficiency Determination for tax years 2020, 2021, and 2022 resulting in $167,543 in entity-level affected business entity tax and interest for 2022), an Idaho S corporation operating since 1993 in structural truss design (using Truswal CAD software) and manufacturing claimed Idaho wage and supply QREs based on a third-party consultant study. Rather than maintaining time or material records, the study consultant conducted brief conversational inquiries with the business owner to estimate a 60%–65% R&D wage allocation (a 35% reduction) and a 20% supply allocation from a commercial "Truss Manufacturing Supplies" cost center.

The Idaho State Tax Commission disallowed the entire credit by synthesizing three federal precedents governing 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2). First, when the petitioner invoked Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201, to justify oral owner estimates without time-tracking records, the Commission noted that Suder primarily addressed whether CEO compensation was unreasonable as a QRE under former IRC § 174(e) compared to similar-sized companies and did not relieve the petitioner of the requirement to establish a documented nexus between employees and specific research tasks. Second, quoting the Seventh Circuit's holding in Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), that "shortcut estimates of experimentation-related activities will not suffice... [s]omething more, such as documentation of time spent on such activities, is necessary," the Commission rejected the 60%–65% conversational wage estimates under IRC § 6001, 26 C.F.R. § 1.6001-1(a), and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(d). Third, applying Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner, 97 T.C.M. (CCH) 1207 (2009), aff'd, 697 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2012), the Commission disallowed the 20% supply estimate (and cutting-floor production wages) because under IRC § 41(d)(2)(C), the truss materials were used to manufacture finished goods sold to customers, were deducted as ordinary cost of goods sold under IRC § 162, and would have been purchased for commercial production regardless of whether any research occurred.
Rhode Island: Correcting the Statutory Citation to R.I. Gen. Laws Section 44-32-3

Rhode Island's Research and Development Expense Credit is actually codified in Title 44, Chapter 32, Section 3 of the Rhode Island General Laws (R.I. Gen. Laws § 44-32-3) (within Chapter 44-32, alongside the § 44-32-1 facilities deduction and the § 44-32-2 R&D property credit).

Under R.I. Gen. Laws § 44-32-3(b)(1), the terms "qualified research expenses" and "base period research expenses" have the exact same meaning as defined in 26 U.S.C. § 41 (encompassing both § 41(b)(2) in-house and § 41(b)(3) contract research expenses, plus a state-specific inclusion for research by property and casualty insurance companies into methods of preventing or reducing losses from fire and other perils), provided that the expenses were incurred in Rhode Island after July 1, 1994. The credit applies against the Rhode Island Business Corporation Tax (R.I. Gen. Laws Ch. 44-11) and Taxation of Insurance Companies / Gross Premiums Tax (Ch. 44-17)—having been repealed for Personal Income Tax (Ch. 44-30) effective January 1, 2011—at a two-tiered marginal rate for amounts paid or accrued after January 1, 1998: 22.5% on excess Rhode Island QREs for the first $25,000 worth of credit taken (corresponding to the first $111,111.11 of excess QREs: $25,000 ÷ 0.225 = $111,111.11), and 16.9% on excess Rhode Island QREs for credit amounts above $25,000. The Rhode Island credit is non-refundable, cannot reduce a corporation's annual tax by more than 50% of pre-credit liability or below the statutory minimum corporate tax under R.I. Gen. Laws § 44-11-2(e), and must be taken into account after the credits under § 44-32-2 and § 44-31-1. Under R.I. Gen. Laws § 44-32-3(c), unused credit amounts carry forward for up to 7 succeeding tax years for prior tax periods, while under R.I. Gen. Laws § 44-32-3(d), for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2026, unused allowable credits may be carried forward for up to 15 succeeding tax years (and while taxpayers must account for federal 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c) elections on their federal returns, the text of R.I. Gen. Laws § 44-32-3 itself contains no explicit reference to IRC § 280C).

Commissioner, noting that statutory IRC § 174(e) was removed by the TCJA for post-2021 years and not re-enacted in IRC § 174A under P.L. 119-21; if $285,000.00 is used as the reasonable CEO wage allocation alongside the unreduced $4,500,000.00 non-executive QREs, the combined federal total is $4,785,000.00). Under the LB&I ASC 730 Directive (LB&I-04-0820-0016 Appendix D), the $3,000,000 combined W-2 wages of the San Francisco QICs ($2,000,000) and Austin direct-support staff ($1,000,000) are included at 95%, yielding $3,000,000 × 0.95 = $2,850,000.00. The CEO (an Upper Level Manager) is capped at 10% of that subtotal: $2,850,000.00 × 0.10 = $285,000.00, yielding $3,135,000.00 in total Directive wage QREs (and disallowing $2,715,000.00 of the CEO's salary plus $150,000.00 of staff wages). Adding the $1,000,000 prototype supplies and $500,000 cloud rental (assuming they are recorded in U.S. ASC 730 accounts) produces an exact ASC 730 Directive federal QRE pool of $2,850,000 + $285,000 + $1,000,000 + $500,000 = $4,635,000.00.

California In-House QRE Pool (R&TC § 23609): Isolating strictly California-situs research (R&TC § 23609(c)(2)), InnovateTech includes the $2,000,000 San Francisco engineering wages, the $600,000 of prototype supplies physically consumed in California, and the reasonable California CEO wage allocation—yielding $2,600,000.00 plus allowable CEO wages under standard substantiation. If applying the ASC 730 Directive ratios, 95% of the $2,000,000 California engineering wages ($1,900,000) plus the $600,000 California supplies plus the San Francisco CEO cap yields $2,785,000.00 (approximately $2.79M) if the full $285,000 federal ULM cap for the San Francisco-based CEO is included, or $2,690,000.00 if the 10% ULM limit is computed solely against the $1,900,000 California staff wage pool ($190,000).

New York In-House QRE Pool (Excelsior Jobs Program / Life Sciences R&D Credit): Isolating strictly New York-situs in-house research, InnovateTech includes the $500,000 NYC AWS cloud computing costs and the $400,000 of prototype supplies physically consumed by NY personnel, totaling $900,000.00. If InnovateTech qualifies as a certified new life sciences business under N.Y. Tax Law § 43 (Form CT-648), its $900,000 of in-house NY QREs generates a fully refundable credit of $135,000.00 at the 15% rate (if employing ≥10 full-time persons) or $180,000.00 at the 20% rate (if employing <10 full-time persons), well within the $500,000 annual cap.

body.text: 7.2 Substantiation Architecture: Automated Engineering Data vs. Retroactive Surveys

While Suder v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2014-201) permitted retrospective percentage allocations under the Cohan rule when backed by detailed, first-hand testimony from an engineering executive, subsequent federal and state decisions—including the Seventh Circuit in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner (62 F.4th 287), the California OTA in Appeal of Electronic Data Systems (2023-OTA-540), and the Idaho State Tax Commission in Docket No. 2-117-100-544—have uniformly rejected unsupported year-end surveys, financial-code ratio assumptions, and brief conversational interviews.

Furthermore, with the IRS's implementation of redesigned Form 6765 (Rev. December 2024), taxpayers required to complete Section G must report qualified wages on a per-business-component basis across Direct Research Wages (Line 50), Direct Supervision Wages (Line 51), and Direct Support Wages (Line 52), alongside component-specific supplies (Line 54) and computer rentals (Line 55). Linking general ledger payroll (IRC § 3401(a)), non-depreciable supply invoices (§ 41(b)(2)(C)), and cloud server environment logs (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(b)(4)) to contemporaneous engineering tickets and commit histories directly substantiates both the 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2) 80% employee wage fraction and the 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6) 80% process-of-experimentation fraction, while geolocating expenditures to satisfy California (R&TC § 23609(c)(2)), New York (N.Y. Tax Law § 43), Idaho (Idaho Code § 63-3029G), and Rhode Island (R.I. Gen. Laws § 44-32-3) situs rules.
